input.question: Why are there so many new medical breakthroughs in the news, but practically none of them ever become legitimate cures.
input.ground_truth: Because a breakthrough towards a cure is just one brick in the road, but it's what gets highly touted by the media because it's easy to point out. A team of scientists working in lab conditions come up with something promising and release their findings. Someone in the media sees this paper and turns "Disease has possible vulnerability!" and turns it into "CURE IS IMMINENT!!!1!" What they don't say is that it will take another few years of research, plus another few years of study, then another few years to create a human-safe cure (doesn't do anyone any good to cure the disease if it kills the patient as well), and then a few more years to figure out how to produce it at profitable levels.

Explain the following question in a simple way as if you are explaining to a 5-year-old.

Question: Why are there so many new medical breakthroughs in the news, but practically none of them ever become legitimate cures.

response.prediction:
Okay! Imagine you are building a big tower with blocks. Every day, you try new ways to stack the blocks higher and higher. Sometimes you find a cool new way to put a block on top, and you tell everyone, “Look! I found a new way!” But just because you found a new way to stack doesn’t mean your tower will never fall down or that it’s the perfect tower forever.

In medicine, scientists are always trying new things to help people feel better. They find new ideas, like new medicines or treatments. These are called “breakthroughs,” like finding a new block trick. But just because something new works a little bit in the beginning doesn’t mean it will always work for everyone, or that it will really, really fix the problem forever. It takes a long time to check if something is truly safe and works for lots of people. So, lots of new ideas are shared, but only a few become real, lasting cures.
